title: SDK latency sculpting and tool-call abstractions (PRD - WIP)
content:
Goal:
Design an SDK-first approach that lets client apps shape perceived latency for streaming responses while preserving correct, typed tool-calling semantics and structured outputs. The focus is on predictable developer ergonomics for mobile/web clients and low-bandwidth environments.

Context and motivation:
- Customers need both low tail latency (fast first token) and high-quality structured results. In many apps the perceived latency matters more than raw throughput.
- Existing hosted-api streaming semantics provide token-by-token streaming, but SDKs are seeing widespread anti-patterns: naive buffering, heavyweight retries of tool calls, and confusion around partial-json fragments.
- We want a small set of SDK abstractions that: 
  * make it straightforward to specify latency budgets per call,
  * let the runtime and SDK negotiate progressive fidelity (fast-first vs full-commit),
  * provide a typed tool-call contract plus an offline/snapshot replay mechanism for deterministic retries.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not attempt to redesign server-side batching or introduce new wire protocols (we assume existing chunked HTTP/WS streaming).
- Not addressing enterprise private-deploy networking specifics in this draft (follow-on doc).

High-level proposals (three complementary levers):
1) Client latency-sculpt API surface (SDK primitives)
- callLatency: optional budget (ms) or preset (fast|balanced|accurate). Default: balanced.
- emissionStrategy: {firstToken: immediate|delayed-by-N-ms, chunked: yes/no} (SDK maps to transport-level buffering).
- partialCommit: flag that accepts progressive structured fragments with a stability marker when the field is final.

2) Tool-call abstraction and lifecycle
- TypedToolCall<TRequest, TResponse> first-class construct.
  * onStart: SDK attaches a local ID and optimistic placeholder result into client UI.
  * resolve: server returns either synchronous tool output or a tool-call handle (tool_handle_id) streamed as part of incremental output.
  * tool-snapshot: SDK can request a compact snapshot for a tool_handle_id to enable deterministic replay if the client is offline and later retries.
- Semantics: tool calls are idempotent if they include the tool_handle_id and a determinism token; otherwise SDK marks as "best-effort".

3) Structured progressive output with stability markers
- Emit partial JSON blocks with small envelope metadata: {path: "document.summary", stable: false|true, seq: X, provenance: [model_id@v]}.
- SDK provides a small parser that merges fragments into an in-memory typed model and exposes a subscription API for UI layers.

Developer ergonomics and patterns:
- High-level SDK methods: streamWithBudget(prompt, options) -> StreamCursor<T>.
  * StreamCursor exposes: onFragment(fn), onStable(fn), currentTypedValue(), pause(), resume(), snapshot().
- Convenience patterns: progressivePreview(plugin) where plugin can render partial structured output into placeholders (e.g., show summary text then replace with final).
- Mobile fallback: SDK will expose a compact "fast-first" mode that emits only firstToken and placeholder JSON schema to save bandwidth and CPU on restore.

Operational behavior & routing notes (for product/infra):
- When callLatency is small (fast), route to fast-capacity pools and enable aggressive prefix-KV cache. When accurate, route to high-accuracy models/quant profiles.
- Servers will annotate fragments with stability flags; SDKs trust stability flag to commit fields to persistent store.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- SDK exposes streamWithBudget and TypedToolCall primitives across JS/TS and Python SDKs.
- Client demo app (React web + small React Native stub) shows: first-token within 200ms on 90th percentile in US region for sample prompt set; structured summary appears progressively and becomes stable.
- Tool-call flow demo: optimistic UI placeholder -> tool_handle id -> snapshot retrieved for retry -> verification of idempotent replay (integration test).

Measurement plan:
- Add telemetry events: sdk.call_latency_budget, sdk.emission_strategy, fragment.stability_time, tool_handle_lifecycle (created/resolved/snapshot_retrieved).
- Key metrics: median time to first fragment, time to stable for top-level fields, % of tool calls resolved synchronously, % of replay failures.

Security and privacy considerations:
- Tool snapshots may contain PII; default snapshot retention is short and encrypted. Admins can opt into longer retention for replay workflows.
- Clients must surface a permission/consent flow when snapshots are stored for later deterministic replay.

Open questions / unknowns (action items):
- What is minimal envelope size for fragments that still allows robust typed merging without large network overhead? (Eng to prototype, HO-312)
- Should stability markers be signed by the control plane to prevent client-side spoofing? (security + infra follow-up)
- How do we expose fallback policies when tool_handle comes from a different region? (ops)

Implementation roadmap (quarterly milestones):
- Q1: API design + JS SDK prototype + sample app demonstrating fast-first and stable fragments.
- Q2: Python SDK parity + server-side fragment stability markers + tool snapshot endpoints.
- Q3: Integration tests, telemetry/dashboard in Console, and opt-in snapshot retention controls.

Next immediate steps (this week):
- Priya: lock API surface and open design RFC in GitHub repo.
- Jordan: spike small JS SDK parser for fragment merging (deliverable: demo app).
- Ethan: infra design doc for fragment stability annotation and routing hints.
- Maya: draft privacy wording for snapshot consent.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: keep the wire protocol unchanged where possible, put complexity in SDK merging logic and runtime routing heuristics.
- Look for edge cases around partial JSON and streaming reconnection semantics.

- [ ] Create Linear tickets for signed stability markers and snapshot retention guardrails.
- [ ] Schedule cross-team sync with security and mobile SDK leads.
